analogy.p: In a Mexican wave each person stands up and sits down in turn. The wave runs round the stadium, but nobody leaves their seat. The people are the particles of the medium and the 'standing' disturbance is the energy being passed on. This also shows a transverse wave, because people move up and down while the wave travels sideways. It breaks down because a real wave passes energy through forces between particles, not because particles can see their neighbours, and a Mexican wave cannot show a longitudinal wave well.

bullets: A wave is produced by a **vibrating source** (a loudspeaker cone, a hand shaking a rope, a dipper in a ripple tank, an oscillating charge).
Energy is passed from particle to particle by the **forces between neighbouring particles**, so each particle copies the motion of the one before it, slightly later.
**Information** (speech, music, TV pictures, Wi-Fi data) is carried by changing a property of the wave, such as its amplitude or frequency.
Because only energy moves, a wave that has travelled a long way is usually **weaker** (lower amplitude) as energy is absorbed or spread out.

The **medium** is the material the wave travels through (air, water, rope, rock). Electromagnetic waves are special because they need **no medium** and can travel through a vacuum (e.g. from the Sun).
Mechanical waves (sound, water, seismic) need a medium; **electromagnetic** waves do not.
core.p: A **wave** is a regular disturbance that carries **energy** from one place to another through a medium (or, for electromagnetic waves, through a vacuum). The key idea in the specification is that **waves transfer energy and information without transferring matter**. The particles of the medium vibrate about a fixed position and pass the energy on to their neighbours, but they do not travel along with the wave. This is why a wave can carry sound or a radio signal across a room without any air or material arriving at the listener from the source.

bullets: Cork on water: moves up and down **perpendicular** to the direction the ripples travel, but stays in the same place overall.
Slinky spring: a coil you push moves forwards and back by a small amount, but the pulse travels the full length of the spring and the coils do not end up at the far end.
Sound: air particles vibrate to and fro about a fixed position; a loudspeaker does not blow air to your ear, it passes on vibrations.
Wave on a rope: a pulse runs along a rope but a ribbon tied to the rope only moves up and down.
Exam wording: 'the wave transfers **energy** from the source to the receiver but there is **no net movement of the particles** of the medium'.
Evidence of energy transfer: waves can do work, e.g. a sound wave makes an eardrum vibrate, light is absorbed and warms a surface, sea waves erode cliffs.
core.h: Waves transfer energy, not matter: the evidence
core.p: The easiest way to see that matter is not transferred is to float a cork (or a ball) on the surface of water and make ripples. The ripples spread out across the surface, but the cork just **bobs up and down on the spot**. If water itself were travelling with the wave, the cork would be carried to the edge of the tank. In the same way, the people in a 'Mexican wave' stand up and sit down while the wave travels round the stadium: nobody moves round the stadium.

bullets: Oscillations ⟂ direction of energy transfer (the symbol ⟂ means 'perpendicular to').
Shape: a repeating up-and-down pattern (a sine-wave shape) with **crests** above and **troughs** below the undisturbed (equilibrium) position.

Examples you must know: **all electromagnetic waves** (radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays), **ripples on the surface of water**, and **waves on a rope or string**.

Transverse waves can travel through solids and along surfaces; they cannot travel through the inside of a gas or liquid as a mechanical wave (EM waves are the exception because they are oscillating electric and magnetic fields).
Seismic **S-waves** are also transverse (they cannot pass through the liquid outer core) - covered in the triple-science seismic waves content.
Water ripples look transverse because the surface moves up and down, though the water particles actually move in small circles.
core.p: In a **transverse wave** the **oscillations (vibrations) are perpendicular (at 90°) to the direction of energy transfer**. Imagine shaking the end of a long rope up and down: the hump travels along the rope, but each piece of rope moves up and down at right angles to the way the wave travels. A transverse wave has high points called **crests (peaks)** and low points called **troughs**.

bullets: Oscillations ∥ direction of energy transfer (∥ means 'parallel to').
A **compression** is a region where the particles are **closer together** than normal, so the pressure is **higher**.
A **rarefaction** is a region where the particles are **further apart** than normal, so the pressure is **lower**.
Examples you must know: **sound waves in air**, **ultrasound**, and **seismic P-waves** (primary waves).
Longitudinal waves need a **medium** because the energy is passed on by particle collisions or bonds: sound cannot travel through a vacuum.
They can travel through **solids, liquids and gases**; in a solid or liquid the particles are closer so sound travels faster than in a gas.
core.p: In a **longitudinal wave** the **oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer**. Push and pull one end of a slinky spring along its length: you create regions where the coils are squashed together and regions where they are stretched apart, and this pattern travels along the spring. The squashed regions are **compressions** and the stretched regions are **rarefactions**.

bullets: Source vibrates -> particles next to it are pushed together (compression) then spread apart (rarefaction).
Each particle moves **parallel** to the direction the wave travels, but returns to its original position.
The **wavelength** of a longitudinal wave is the distance from the centre of one compression to the centre of the next (or rarefaction to rarefaction).
The **frequency** is how many compressions pass a point each second; the **amplitude** is linked to how much the particles are displaced (louder sound = larger amplitude).
Typical speed of sound in air is about **330 m/s** (it is much faster in water and solids).
Sound can be drawn on an oscilloscope as a transverse-looking wave, but this graph shows pressure or displacement against time, **not** the shape of the real wave.
core.h: How a sound wave works (longitudinal in detail)
core.p: A loudspeaker cone moves forwards and backwards. When it moves forward it squashes the air in front into a **compression**; when it moves back it leaves a **rarefaction**. These alternate compressions and rarefactions move away from the speaker at the speed of sound. Each air particle only vibrates a tiny distance to and fro about its rest position, passing the pressure change on to the next particle. When the wave reaches your ear it makes the eardrum vibrate at the same frequency, which your brain detects as sound.

bullets: **Amplitude**: the maximum displacement of a point on a wave away from its undisturbed (rest) position. On a transverse wave it is measured from the middle line to a crest (or trough), **not** from crest to trough.

**Wavelength (λ)**: the distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave, e.g. crest to crest, trough to trough, or compression to compression. Measured in **metres (m)**.
**Frequency (f)**: the number of waves passing a point each second. Measured in **hertz (Hz)**; 1 Hz = 1 wave per second.
**Period (T)**: the time taken for one complete wave to pass a point, T = 1 ÷ f, measured in seconds.
Amplitude relates to **energy**: a bigger amplitude means a more energetic wave (louder sound, brighter light, taller water wave).
Wavelength and frequency are related by the wave speed: v = f × λ (see the wave equation note).
core.h: Describing a wave: amplitude, wavelength, frequency, period
core.p: The specification asks you to describe wave motion in terms of four quantities. These apply to **both** transverse and longitudinal waves. They are defined precisely in the next topics, but you must be able to recognise them straight away on a diagram.

bullets: Transverse: oscillations **perpendicular**; features are **crests and troughs**; examples EM waves, water ripples, waves on a rope.
Longitudinal: oscillations **parallel**; features are **compressions and rarefactions**; examples sound, ultrasound, P-waves.
Transverse mechanical waves need a medium with some rigidity (solid or surface); **longitudinal waves** can travel in any state of matter.
EM waves are transverse and **can travel through a vacuum**; sound (longitudinal) **cannot**.
Both transfer **energy without transferring matter**.
Both can be reflected, refracted and diffracted, and both have measurable wavelength, frequency, amplitude and speed.
core.p: The exam often asks you to compare the two types, so learn a clear side-by-side list. The only difference that matters in the definition is the **direction of the oscillations relative to the direction of energy transfer**. Everything else (wavelength, frequency, amplitude, speed = frequency × wavelength) works the same way.

bullets: Choose two points that are in the **same stage** of the cycle (same displacement and moving in the same direction).
Measuring several wavelengths and dividing is more accurate: if 5 successive crests are 1.2 m apart overall, there are **4 gaps**, so λ = 1.2 ÷ 4 = 0.30 m.
Crest to adjacent trough = **λ/2**.
On a longitudinal wave, compression to adjacent rarefaction = **λ/2**.
Always give the unit and read from a scale at eye level to avoid parallax error.
If a diagram shows distance along the horizontal axis, read wavelength from the **displacement-distance graph**; read the period from a **displacement-time graph**.
core.h: Measuring wavelength on each wave type
core.p: Where you measure wavelength depends on the wave type, and examiners like to test this. On a transverse wave you can measure from crest to crest or trough to trough. On a longitudinal wave you measure from the centre of a compression to the centre of the next compression. A common error is to measure the distance between **one crest and the next trough**, which is only **half** a wavelength.

bullets: Transverse on slinky: shake the end sideways; the pulse looks like a hump moving along the coils.
Longitudinal on slinky: push-pull along the length; bunched coils = compression, spread coils = rarefaction.
A ribbon or marker on a coil shows the **particle motion** compared with the **wave motion**.
In both cases the wave travels the length of the slinky but the coils return to their start positions.
Link: the same demonstration is used to explain why sound needs a medium (the 'coils' are the air particles).
Safety/accuracy: keep the slinky taut and low, do not overstretch it, and use a long enough distance to time the pulse.
core.h: Waves on a rope and slinky: demonstrations
core.p: Two classic demonstrations let you show both wave types with the same equipment. Fix a slinky spring on a smooth bench. Moving one end **side to side** (at 90° to the spring) gives a **transverse** wave. Pushing and pulling one end **along the length** of the spring gives a **longitudinal** wave with compressions (coils bunched up) and rarefactions (coils spread out). Tying a ribbon to a coil shows that the coil only vibrates about a fixed position.

bullets: EM waves transfer energy from the source to an absorber (e.g. the Sun warms the Earth, a microwave oven heats food).
Because they are transverse they can be **polarised** (not required at GCSE, but it is the evidence for them being transverse).
They travel through a **vacuum**, unlike sound.
EM spectrum order (low to high frequency): radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.
All are transverse and travel at the same speed in a vacuum, but different wavelengths and frequencies give different properties and uses.
Do not confuse EM waves (transverse) with sound waves (longitudinal): a favourite exam trap.
core.p: All electromagnetic waves are transverse. They are made of oscillating electric and magnetic fields that are at right angles to each other and to the direction the wave travels, so no particles are needed. This is why light from the Sun reaches the Earth through space. All EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum (about 3.0 × 10^8 m/s) and differ in wavelength and frequency; this is developed in the EM spectrum topics.

bullets: **Reflection, refraction and diffraction** apply to both wave types and are shown in a ripple tank.
**Ultrasound** (frequency above 20 000 Hz) is longitudinal and is used in medical imaging and industrial testing.
**Seismic waves**: P-waves longitudinal and travel through solids and liquids; S-waves transverse and only through solids.
**Sound** in different media: speed is greater in solids than in air because particles are closer together and pass vibrations on faster.
The **wave equation** v = f × λ applies to every wave type.
**Energy transfer**: a loudspeaker transfers electrical energy to the kinetic energy of air particles.
core.h: Why this matters: links to other topics
core.p: Knowing the type of wave helps you explain what happens in later topics. For example, ultrasound used in medical scanning is a longitudinal wave that reflects at boundaries between tissues; seismic P-waves (longitudinal) and S-waves (transverse) travelling through the Earth give evidence for its liquid core; sound reflecting from a wall gives echoes; light reflecting from a mirror obeys the same law as water waves bouncing off a barrier in a ripple tank.

bullets: To classify an unfamiliar wave, compare the **direction of vibration** with the **direction of travel**.
Explain why sound cannot travel in a vacuum: there are **no particles** to vibrate and pass on the energy.
Explain why EM waves can: they are oscillations of fields and need no particles.
In triple science, the behaviour of P- and S-waves is used to deduce the **structure of the Earth**.
A graph can show displacement or pressure against distance for **either** type of wave, so the graph alone does not tell you the type: you need the description.
Be able to sketch and label a transverse wave (crest, trough, amplitude, wavelength) and a longitudinal wave (compression, rarefaction, wavelength).
core.p: At Higher tier you are expected to explain the same ideas in more depth and apply them to unfamiliar situations. You may be asked to decide from a description or diagram whether a wave is transverse or longitudinal, to justify the choice using the direction of oscillation, and to explain why a particular wave can or cannot pass through a medium (e.g. why S-waves cannot travel through the Earth's liquid outer core).

exam: 'State' / 'Name' (1 mark): give one precise word, e.g. 'longitudinal'.

'Describe the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves' (2 marks): one mark for each correctly linked statement: 'transverse: oscillations perpendicular to direction of energy transfer; longitudinal: oscillations parallel'.
Give an **example** for each (1 mark each): transverse - EM waves/water ripples/rope; longitudinal - sound/ultrasound/P-waves.
'Explain how a wave transfers energy' (2-3 marks): particles vibrate, pass energy to neighbours, particles do not move with the wave (no net movement).
For a floating-cork question, the full-mark phrase is 'the cork moves up and down but does not travel with the wave, so the wave transfers energy but not matter'.
Label questions: use the exact words crest, trough, compression, rarefaction, amplitude, wavelength; draw the amplitude from the **middle line**.
Use a ruler for wavelength: count the number of waves and divide the distance by the number of **wavelengths** (not number of crests).
4-mark 'describe how to show a longitudinal wave on a slinky': push/pull along the length, identify compressions and rarefactions, ribbon shows coils only move to and fro.
Give units in numerical answers: m for wavelength and amplitude, Hz for frequency, s for period.
6-mark extended answers: define both types, give examples, link to direction of oscillation, mention energy not matter, then link to a use (sound/ultrasound/EM).

mistakes.r: Particles only oscillate about a fixed position; the wave transfers energy, not matter.
mistakes.w: Particles of water or air travel along with the wave.

mistakes.r: Define by direction relative to energy transfer: transverse = perpendicular, longitudinal = parallel.
mistakes.w: Transverse waves go up and down; longitudinal waves go side to side.

mistakes.r: Sound is longitudinal, with compressions and rarefactions; it needs a medium.
Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the undisturbed (middle) position, half the crest-to-trough height.
mistakes.w: Amplitude is the distance from crest to trough.

mistakes.r: Wavelength is crest to the next crest (or equivalent points); crest to trough is half a wavelength.
mistakes.w: Wavelength is the distance from a crest to the next trough.

mistakes.r: Light is an electromagnetic wave and travels through a vacuum.
mistakes.w: Light needs air to travel through.

mistakes.r: A compression is where particles are close together and pressure is high; it is a longitudinal feature.
mistakes.w: A compression is where the waves are high.

mistakes.r: The cork vibrates up and down in the same place; only energy moves.
mistakes.w: The wave moves the cork across the water.

summary: You must know that waves transfer energy and information without transferring matter, and be able to describe and give examples of transverse waves (oscillations perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer) and longitudinal waves (oscillations parallel to it, with compressions and rarefactions). This is the foundation for every other Waves topic: sound, light, the electromagnetic spectrum, ultrasound and seismic waves all depend on knowing which type of wave you are dealing with.

terms.d: A disturbance that transfers energy (and information) from one place to another without transferring matter.
The substance a mechanical wave travels through, e.g. air, water, a rope.
A wave in which the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
A wave in which the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer; it shows compressions and rarefactions.
A region in a longitudinal wave where the particles are closer together, giving higher pressure.
A region in a longitudinal wave where the particles are further apart, giving lower pressure.
The highest point of a transverse wave, a point of maximum positive displacement.
The lowest point of a transverse wave, a point of maximum negative displacement.
The maximum displacement of a point on a wave away from its undisturbed position.
The distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave.
The number of waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz).
The time taken for one complete wave to pass a point; period = 1 ÷ frequency.
A repeated to-and-fro (back and forth or up and down) movement about a fixed position.
A transverse wave made of oscillating electric and magnetic fields that can travel through a vacuum.
Sound waves with a frequency higher than the upper limit of human hearing (above 20 000 Hz).
The position of a particle or point when no wave is passing (equilibrium position).

worked.ans: In a transverse wave the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer, for example light waves. In a longitudinal wave the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer and the wave has compressions and rarefactions, for example sound waves.
worked.q: Describe the difference between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave and give one example of each. [4 marks]
steps: Define transverse: oscillations are perpendicular (90°) to the direction of energy transfer.
Define longitudinal: oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
Example of transverse: light (any EM wave), ripples on water or a wave on a rope.
Example of longitudinal: sound waves or ultrasound or P-waves.

worked.ans: 0.30 m (not 1.20 ÷ 5 = 0.24 m, which is a common mistake).
worked.q: A student measures the distance between 5 successive compressions of a sound wave on a slinky as 1.20 m. Calculate the wavelength. [2 marks]
steps: 5 successive compressions have 5 - 1 = 4 gaps between them.
Each gap is one wavelength, so λ = total distance ÷ number of gaps.

worked.ans: The cork bobs up and down in the same place, perpendicular to the direction the ripples travel. It is not carried across the pond, which shows that the wave transfers energy without transferring matter.
worked.q: A cork floats on a pond. Ripples pass it. Describe and explain the motion of the cork and what this shows about waves. [3 marks]
steps: State the motion: the cork moves up and down (vibrates) about a fixed position.
Link to wave direction: this is at right angles to the direction the ripples move.
Conclusion: the cork is not carried along, so waves transfer energy but not matter.
